title: Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency: An Empirical Study of Two-Stage Branch Budgeting for LLM Reasoning

contributions.purpose: Investigate whether adaptive compute allocation to promising branches can improve self-consistency efficiency.
contributions.mechanism: Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS): Stage 1 samples B=7 short drafts (T_draft=1024), extracts interim answers, and builds a vote histogram; Stage 2 selects k=3 high-vote branches and continues them for T_cont=1024 more tokens using a hedge allocation that reserves one slot for the second-place answer; final answer by majority vote.
contributions.evaluation: Presented as a two-stage method with ~10,240 token budget per problem; sampling temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95.
contributions.domain: LLM mathematical reasoning / test-time compute allocation
contributions.source_quote: We introduce Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve efficiency by continuing promising branches rather than stopping early.

contributions.purpose: Rigorously compare DCS against standard and efficient self-consistency baselines.
contributions.mechanism: Evaluate on MATH-500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct against Greedy CoT, Uniform SC (n=5), and CGES-LNS (confidence-guided early stopping), over 3 seeds, reporting accuracy, average tokens, and API calls.
contributions.evaluation: DCS reaches 76.8% accuracy, matching Uniform SC (76.67%) and CGES-LNS (76.8%) but using 4114.5 tokens: 19.6% more than Uniform SC and 109% more than CGES-LNS; higher variance (0.75%).
contributions.source_quote: We conduct rigorous experiments on MATH-500 comparing DCS against greedy decoding, uniform self-consistency, and confidence-guided early stopping.

contributions.purpose: Explain the negative result and derive a general condition under which two-stage budgeting fails.
contributions.mechanism: Diagnostic analysis of draft completion rate and fallback fraction; argue effectiveness depends on the relationship between draft length and problem complexity.
contributions.evaluation: ~96.3% of drafts complete within T_draft=1024 (fallback only 3.73%), so the continuation stage rarely activates and DCS degenerates into overhead-laden self-consistency; CGES-LNS Pareto-dominates DCS (identical accuracy, 52% fewer tokens, 2.48 vs ~10 calls).
contributions.source_quote: We report a negative result with detailed analysis: DCS fails to improve efficiency because high draft completion rates (~96%) undermine the continuation mechanism, demonstrating that simpler early-stopping methods dominate two-stage approaches when draft budgets are sufficient.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) exemplifies this approach by sampling multiple chain-of-thought reasoning paths (Wei et al., 2022) and aggregating answers via majority vote.

While effective, these approaches fundamentally discard partial reasoning—they stop sampling entirely rather than leveraging the information contained in incomplete chains. This raises a natural question: can we identify promising reasoning paths early and focus continuation budget on them?
Our Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency differs from early-stopping methods by attempting to continue promising branches rather than simply terminating sampling.
CGES-LNS (Aghazadeh et al., 2025): confidence-guided early stopping with length-normalized scoring, b_max = 5 maximum samples, and confidence threshold gamma = 0.95.

notes: This is an explicitly negative-result paper: DCS matches baseline accuracy but is strictly worse on efficiency (19.6% more tokens than Uniform SC, 109% more than CGES-LNS which Pareto-dominates it) and has higher variance. Authors note limitations: single dataset, single model, untuned hyperparameters.
